essence: Clarice decays and flourishes again and again, and all that survives each turn is its name, its site and a fixed set of hard-to-break objects, shuffled into new uses every age, so that no one can prove there ever was a first Clarice.
textDetails: Clarice is a glorious city with a turbulent past; it has declined and revived several times.
Through all of it the first Clarice serves as the incomparable model of splendour, and the current city prompts new sighs with every wheeling of the stars.
During its long decline plague emptied it; falling beams, cornices and slides of earth cut down its height; neglect and absent upkeep left it rusted and choked.
Survivors crept back out of basements and burrows in swarms, rat-like in their urge to scavenge and gnaw, bird-like in their urge to gather and patch nests.
Anything portable was carried off and reused: brocade curtains became bedsheets.
Basil grew in marble urns made to hold the ashes of the dead.
Wrought-iron window grilles ripped from the women's quarters (the harem) became grills for roasting cat meat over fires of inlaid wood.

The result, cobbled from the scraps of the old city, was a city of survival: shacks and hovels, open sewers, rabbit hutches; yet nearly all the old splendour was still there, merely rearranged in an order that met people's needs just as well.

Lean times gave way to merrier ones: a splendid butterfly Clarice broke out of the ragged chrysalis Clarice, overflowing with new materials, buildings and goods, and with newcomers who had no tie to any earlier Clarice.

The more the new city triumphantly occupied the old one's site and name, the more it sensed it was drifting from it and wrecking it as quickly as vermin and mould had; for all its pride it felt like a stranger, out of place, an impostor.

The relics of the first splendour, which had survived by serving humble purposes, were relocated again: placed under glass domes, in locked vitrines, on velvet cushions, no longer for use but in the hope of reconstructing a city nobody remembered.
Further cycles of decay and abundance followed, with populations and customs changing again and again; only the name, the location and the least breakable objects stay.
Every new Clarice is as compact as a living organism, with its own odours and breathing, and wears the dead fragments of former Clarices like a jewel.

Nobody knows when the Corinthian capitals were on top of columns; a single one is remembered because for years, in a chicken coop, it propped up the basket in which hens laid eggs, before joining the row of specimens in the Museum of Capitals.

The sequence of the eras is lost; belief in an original Clarice is common but unproven: the capitals might have stood in coops before temples, the urns might have grown basil before holding human bones.

The only certainty: a fixed stock of objects moves around a fixed space, sometimes buried under new things, sometimes wearing out unreplaced, and the rule is to reshuffle them every time and attempt to fit them together again; maybe Clarice was always just a muddle of chipped, mismatched, useless trinkets.
visualConcept: Clarice is a fixed site and a fixed hand of cards. A round plinth of old travertine, the site that never changes, bears the name CLARICE cut around its rim and carries a counted set of durable fragments that persist through every age: 9 Corinthian capitals, 12 marble cinerary urns, 8 wrought-iron window grilles and 6 brocade curtains, all rendered more crisply and a touch brighter than anything around them (clean marble, black iron, crimson-and-gold damask) so the eye can follow them. Around them, the perishable city of each age is grown and dissolved. In the chrysalis Clarice, the survivors' city, a low tangle of patched huts crowds the plinth among fallen beams, broken cornice blocks and landslip mounds; basil sprouts from the urns at the thresholds, grilles lie across small fires of inlaid wood, brocade is spread as bedsheets, rabbit cages are stacked, dark rivulets fester in the lanes, rats stream and birds patch nests, and one capital stands in a chicken run holding up the hens' egg basket. In the butterfly Clarice, glossy new buildings of glass, enamel and polished metal crowd in, sharp and faintly garish, and the same fragments become relics: urns under glass bells on velvet cushions, grilles and brocade locked in display cases, the capitals in a row in the long, top-lit Museum of Capitals with the egg-basket capital among them. Above it all, never solid, hangs the first Clarice everyone sighs for: a faint gold line-drawing of colonnades with capitals on their columns, a palace of grilled windows and a terrace of urns, a model with no proof. Under a slowly wheeling dome of stars the fragments are lifted, shuffled in the air and dealt again into the other city.
layout: Plinth radius 21, top at y=0, travertine with cracks and patches; CLARICE cut into the rim face in letters 1.2 tall. Fixed inventory, identical in count in every state: 9 capitals (0.6 tall: lathe body, two rings of extruded acanthus leaves, corner volutes), 12 urns (0.5 tall, lathe), 8 grilles (0.8 by 1.1 lattices of thin bars and scroll arcs), 6 brocade cloths (1.4 by 1, cloth shader with a damask pattern). The chicken run and the Museum of Capitals occupy the same spot, centre-front at (0, 0, 4), in both states. Chrysalis: about 70 huts (0.5-1.2 tall, irregular and leaning) packed in an uneven ring between r=4 and r=17 along muddy lanes; 6 fires with grilles laid across them; 12 urn-planters with basil at doorways; 6 brocade sheets on low beds or drying lines; 10 stacks of rabbit cages; fallen beams and about 15 cornice blocks scattered; 3 landslip mounds at the rim; dark rivulets running outward; the chicken run (a 2 by 2 fence) with one capital holding a basket and 5 hens, the other 8 capitals serving as seats, steps and props. Butterfly: about 40 new buildings (1.5-5 tall: glass pavilions, enamelled towers, a domed arcade, bright awnings) on a regular grid; the Museum of Capitals, an open-roofed gallery 8 by 2.4 with 9 plinths in a line; 12 bell jars on velvet cushions on pedestals along a promenade; 8 grille cases and 6 brocade cases. Ghost first Clarice: an additive line drawing between y=7 and y=14 over a footprint of radius 14: a temple with 9 columns crowned by capitals, a palace with 8 grilled windows hung with brocade, a necropolis terrace with 12 urns. Star dome of radius 60 overhead.
signatureMotion: 1) The shuffle (on toggle, about 7 s): the perishable buildings crumble to dust (chrysalis) or splinter into glassy shards that sink (butterfly); all 35 fragments rise, tumble slowly and circle in a loose vortex 4-8 units above the plinth, overtaking one another and swapping orbits like a deck being shuffled; they hang for a breath as a floating jumble of chipped knick-knacks, then descend one by one into their new places and uses while the next age's buildings grow up around them. 2) The sigh: the star dome turns once every 40 s, and at each completed turn the ghostly first Clarice brightens and fades like a held breath. 3) The living city: in the chrysalis, fires flicker under the grilles, threads of smoke rise, rats stream along the rivulets, birds flit from roof to roof with scraps; in the butterfly, crowds drift past the vitrines and highlights travel over the bell jars; in either age the perishable city swells almost imperceptibly (about 1 percent every 6 s), compact as a breathing body.
interactionDescription: Toggles between the chrysalis Clarice (the survivors' city of huts, where the fragments are put to use) and the butterfly Clarice (the new city of glass and gilt, where the very same fragments sit under bell jars, in display cases and in the Museum of Capitals). Each toggle runs the shuffle: the same 35 objects lift, tumble, hang for a moment as a jumble and land in new roles, never more and never fewer. The faint gold first Clarice above never becomes solid in either state.
mood: Evening under a deep verdigris sky with a dusty amber band at the horizon and a slowly wheeling dome of stars. Chrysalis: low, smoky and ember-lit, a haze of cooking smoke, browns and rust with small warm points of fire. Butterfly: crisp, bright and lacquered, cool white glass light and gilt reflections, a sparkle on every bell jar. In both, the fragments are lit a little brighter than their surroundings, like objects in a reliquary; basil green and deep velvet blue are the only other strong colours.
caption: Clarice has fallen and risen more times than anyone can count, and each time it sighs for a first Clarice that no one can prove was ever there. In lean years survivors sleep in brocade, grow basil in burial urns and grill their meat on lattices pried off the harem's windows; in rich years the same pieces go under glass. Only the name, the ground and a few unbreakable things remain, shuffled and dealt again.
motto: Same name, same pieces; every age deals a different city.
camera: Distance about 44, elevation about 18 degrees, target (0, 3, 0), vertical field of view about 40 degrees: the whole plinth fills the lower two-thirds with the chicken-run and Museum of Capitals spot just below frame centre, and the ghostly first Clarice hangs in the band of sky just above the plinth's far edge, under the turning stars; slow orbit, one turn per 3 minutes; during the shuffle the camera pulls back about 10 percent and tilts up slightly to hold the whole vortex.
